# Job arrays: the feature that changes how you work {#sec-arrays}

::: {.tldr}
A job array runs the *same script* hundreds or thousands of times, each with a different
index (`$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID`). One `sbatch`, one script, N independent tasks that the
scheduler spreads across the cluster and backfills into gaps. For parameter sweeps,
ensembles, and per-file processing, this is the single biggest productivity unlock on the
machine. MedicineBow allows arrays up to **10,000** tasks.
:::

## The problem it solves

You have 500 fire-weather scenarios to run, or 500 input tiles to process. The wrong way is a
bash loop that runs them one after another in a single job (serial, slow, and one crash near
the end wastes everything). The other wrong way is copy-pasting 500 submit scripts. The right
way is **one array job**: one script, submitted once, that Slurm turns into 500 independent
tasks it can run in parallel and backfill wherever there's room.

## The mechanics

Add `--array` and use `$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID` to pick which piece of work this task does:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=cowy-firesurro
#SBATCH --job-name=sweep
#SBATCH --array=1-500                 # 500 tasks, indices 1..500
#SBATCH --qos=fast                    # short independent tasks → high-priority QOS
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00               # per task
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --output=logs/sweep-%A_%a.out # %A = array job id, %a = task index

module purge
module load gcc/14.2.0 python/3.12.0

# Use the task index to select this task's work:
python run_scenario.py --scenario-id ${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}
```

Submit once:

```bash
mkdir -p logs
sbatch submit_array.sh        # creates 500 tasks: 12345_1, 12345_2, ... 12345_500
```

Each task is scheduled independently. Because they're small and short, they **backfill
beautifully** (@sec-priority) and the whole sweep can finish far faster than the sum of its
parts.

## Driving work from the index

The index is just a number; you map it to real work. Common patterns:

**Line N of a parameter file:**

```bash
PARAM=$(sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p" params.txt)
python run.py $PARAM
```

**The Nth input file:**

```bash
FILES=(/project/cowy-firesurro/data/tiles/*.tif)
THIS=${FILES[$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID]}      # note: arrays are 0-indexed in bash
python process.py "$THIS"
```

(If you index files from a bash array, start `--array=0`; if you use `sed -n Np`, start
`--array=1`. Off-by-one here is the classic array bug.)

## Throttling: be a good neighbor

Don't necessarily unleash all 500 at once — cap how many run simultaneously with `%`:

```bash
#SBATCH --array=1-500%20        # at most 20 tasks running at a time
```

This keeps you from saturating your account's core cap (and your fair-share, @sec-priority),
while still churning through all 500. A modest `%` limit is often *faster overall* because you
stop competing with yourself and stay backfill-friendly.

## Managing an array

```bash
squeue --me                     # shows pending tasks collapsed, e.g. 12345_[6-500]
scancel 12345                   # cancel the whole array
scancel 12345_7                 # cancel just task 7
sacct -j 12345                  # per-task outcomes after the fact
```

To find which tasks failed (so you can rerun only those):

```bash
sacct -j 12345 --format=JobID,State,ExitCode -n | grep -v COMPLETED
```

then resubmit just those indices: `sbatch --array=17,43,88 submit_array.sh`.

::: {.callout-note}
## Arrays vs. one big MPI job
An array is for **independent** tasks that don't talk to each other (embarrassingly
parallel): sweeps, ensembles, per-file pipelines. If your tasks must communicate — a single
domain-decomposed simulation — that's an **MPI** job instead (@sec-ladder), a different tool
for a different shape of problem.
:::

Arrays are also the natural unit for **ensembles** in fire/atmospheric work: one array task
per ensemble member, each writing to its own output, collected afterward. Reach for them
early — most "I need to run this many times" problems are secretly array jobs.
